raw_response:
I am 58 years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou for over 40 years. I have 7 mu of good flat land with well water. My body is not what it used to be — my back bothers me when I bend too long — so I cannot take on crops that need endless pesticides or risky market trips. I also do not trust new-fangled schemes; middle school was enough education to teach me that steady and simple beats flashy and uncertain.

This year, I will stick to the wheat–maize rotation on all 7 mu. It is what my father did, what my neighbors do, and what the grain station still buys without haggling. Winter wheat gives me grain for the household and steady cash from the surplus, and summer maize follows it naturally after the June harvest. I thought about cotton because the price looked tempting last autumn, but I remembered the 12–13 times I would have to spray insecticide, and my shoulders said no. Vegetables pay more, but one bad rain or one dishonest broker and you are left with rotten tomatoes and an empty pocket. At my age, I want sleep at night, not worry.

For the winter wheat, I will sow *Jimai 22* — an improved variety that the seed shop in town always stocks. It is not the newest name, but I know it: it stands up to the dry spring winds and does not lodge if I irrigate on time. I will rotary-till the field after the October corn stalks are chopped and spread. Basal fertilizer will be a compound bag (the 18-22-5 blend) at 100 kg per mu, and I will broadcast urea at green-up and again at jointing. I will irrigate four times: the winter freeze water, the green-up water, the jointing water, and one more at grain filling. The well pump is old but reliable. For pests, I will spray insecticide twice — once at the wheat awn stage and once if aphids show up — and lay down herbicide before sowing. I expect about 1,000 jin per mu, maybe a bit more if the spring rain cooperates.

For the summer maize, I will plant *Denghai 605*, a hybrid seed. Everyone here uses it; the ears are thick and the stalks stay green late. I will no-till sow directly into the wheat stubble right after harvest — no time to waste in June, and the stubble mulch keeps the soil moist. One basal compound application (the 27-6-7 blend, about 90 kg per mu) is enough; the wheat residue already left some nitrogen behind. I will irrigate twice: once when the tassels emerge and once during grain filling. Maize needs less water than wheat if the summer rain is normal. I will spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. If the weather is average, I should get 1,150 jin per mu.

I will keep a small home garden by the house for tomatoes and scallions for the kitchen, but that does not count as real crop land. The rest of my decision is simple: do what the land knows, do what my back can handle, and sell the grain when the price is fair.
